question: Among the five meta-analyses in this corpus, which reported significantly longer robotic operative time, and what estimates did they report?
answer: Muafa: MD +23.8 min (95% CI 14.2–33.4); Gahunia: SMD 0.57 (0.31–0.83) obesity, 0.77 (0.17–1.37) male, 0.50 (0.18–0.83) elderly, 0.48 (0.12–0.84) low rectal tumours, 0.72 (0.34–1.09) neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, 1.55 (0.05–3.06) previous surgery; Morini: MD 62.47 (95% CI 18.17, 106.76) min; Al-Ihribat: colon MD 39.64 (28.05–51.23) min and rectum MD 47.58 (28.19–66.98) min, but colorectal subgroup not significant; Zou: MD 23.46 (15.76, 31.16) min.
quote: Pooled analysis using random-effects models showed that RAS required significantly longer operative time compared with LS:MD = + 23.8 min (95% CI 14.2–33.4; I² = 67%).

A meta-analysis including the seven studies which reported operative time found significantly longer operations using robotic-assisted surgery (SMD 0.57 [CI 0.31–0.83], p < 0.0001). Nine studies reported conversion-to-open rates, and meta-analysis demonstrated a significantly lower conversion rate in robotic-assisted surgery (OR 0.41 [CI 0.32–0.51], p < 0.00001). Six studies reported on length of stay, and meta-analysis suggested a reduced length of stay in patients undergoing robotic-assisted surgery (SMD 0.25 [CI − 0.41 to − 0.09], p = 0.002). Blood loss (SMD 0.23 [CI − 0.51 to 0.05], p = 0.11), overall complication rate (OR 0.96 [CI 0.81–1.14], p = 0.68), and lymph node yield (SMD 0.11 [CI − 0.07 to 0.28], p = 0.24) were comparable between groups.

Four studies examined male gender as a high-risk factor and included a total of 934 robotic-assisted cases and 3762 laparoscopic cases [24, 29, 42, 43]. All but one of the studies looked at resections for rectal cancer alone, with the fourth study including all types of colectomies. There were no significant differences between the two groups with regards to complication rate (OR 1.09 [CI 0.91–1.30], p = 0.36) or length of stay (SMD 0.19 [CI − 0.51–0.13], p = 0.25). Operative time was again significantly longer in the robotic-assisted group (SMD 0.77 [CI 0.17–1.37], p = 0.01). However, conversion to open was significantly lower in the robotic-assisted group (OR 0.28 [CI 0.22–0.34], p < 0.00001), Fig. 3.

Operative time was significantly longer in the robotic-assisted group (SMD 0.50 [CI 0.18–0.83], p = 0.002). There was no difference between the two groups with regards to conversion to open (OR 0.28 [CI 0.07–1.11], p = 0.07), complication rate (OR 1.02 [CI 0.59–1.78], p = 0.94), length of stay (SMD 3.20 [CI − 10.45 to 4.06], p = 0.39), estimated blood loss (SMD 0.04 [CI − 0.29 to 0.22], p = 0.77) or lymph node yield (SMD 0.34 [CI − 0.78 to 0.10], p = 0.13).

Operative time was significantly longer in the robotic-assisted group (SMD 0.48 [CI 0.12–0.84], p = 0.008), Fig. 3. There was no difference between the two groups with regards to complication rate (OR 0.94 [CI 0.58–1.52], p = 0.81), estimated blood loss (SMD − 0.37 [CI − 0.89 to 0.15], p = 0.16), length of stay (SMD − 0.34 [CI − 0.87 to 0.18], p = 0.20) or lymph node yield SMD − 0.07 [CI − 0.34 to 0.19], p = 0.59).

Seven studies examined patients who had received long-course neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for low rectal cancer, with a total number of 305 robotic-assisted cases and 422 laparoscopic [26, 32, 33, 41, 43, 47, 53], Fig. 3. Operative time was significantly longer in the robotic-assisted group (SMD 0.72 [CI 0.34–1.09], p = 0.0002). There was no difference between the two groups with regards to conversion to open (OR 0.47 [CI 0.09–2.43], p = 0.37), complication rate (OR 1.10 [CI 0.66–1.81], p = 0.72), estimated blood loss (SMD 0.17 [CI − 0.74 to 0.40], p = 0.56), length of stay (SMD 0.07 [CI − 0.22 to 0.08], p = 0.36) or lymph node yield (SMD 0.18 [CI − 0.28 to 0.64], p = 0.44).

Two studies looked at patients who had previous abdominal surgery, with a total number of 274 robotic-assisted cases and 674 laparoscopic [35, 39]. There was no significant difference between the two groups with regards to conversion to open (OR 0.42 [CI 0.08–2.21], p = 0.30), complication rate (OR 0.89 [CI 0.35–2.27], p = 0.80) or length of stay (SMD 0.06 [CI − 0.14 to 0.27], p = 0.54). Again, operative time was significantly longer for RAS (SMD 1.55 [CI 0.05–3.06], p = 0.04), Fig. 3.

The Overall Operative Time (OOT) was examined by all four studies included in our meta-analysis, involving 373 patients: 116 in the RC group and 257 in the LC group [19–22] Fig. 2. Upon examining the pooled results on the overall operative time, obtained from the meta-analysis, a statistically significant difference emerged between the groups under consideration [mean difference (MD): 62.47, 95% confidence interval (CI): 18.17, 106.76, P=0.006]. The observed I2 value was 92% (high heterogeneity), with a p-value of <0.00001, which was statistically significant.Fig. 2Forest plot comparing overall operative time between the RC and LC groups. SD, standard deviation; IV, inverse variance; CI, confidence interval; RC, Robotic colectomy; LC, Laparoscopic colectomy

Subgroup analysis of six studies in the colon subgroup revealed that robotic-assisted surgery took significantly longer operative time compared to conventional laparoscopic surgery [Mean Difference (MD): 39.64 min; 95% CI: 28.05–51.23; p < 0.001; I2 = 97.5%] (Figure 3). Similarly, in the rectum subgroup (10 studies), robotic-assisted operations lasted significantly longer operative times (MD: 47.58 min; 95% CI: 28.19–66.98; p < 0.001; I2 = 97.8%). In contrast, the colorectal subgroup (4 studies) no statistically significant difference was observed in the operative time between the two approaches (MD: 7.93 min; 95% CI: −11.16 to 27.29; p = 0.42; I2 = high).

note: Scope is all five meta-analysis papers in papers.jsonl. Gahunia and Al-Ihribat report subgroup estimates rather than one overall pooled estimate; the colorectal subgroup in Al-Ihribat was not significant.

question: Among the five meta-analyses in this corpus, which found a statistically significant reduction in conversion with robotic surgery, and what were their reported pooled estimates or subgroups?
answer: Muafa: OR 0.42 (95% CI 0.28–0.63); Gahunia: obesity OR 0.41 (0.32–0.51), male OR 0.28 (0.22–0.34), low rectal tumours OR 0.10 (0.02–0.58); Al-Ihribat: colon RR 0.62 (0.52–0.74) and rectum RR 0.44 (0.34–0.59), but colorectal subgroup not significant; Zou: OR 0.42 (0.28–0.63). Morini found no significant difference: OR 0.20 (0.04, 1.14), P=0.07.
quote: Robotic surgery showed a significantly lower conversion rate:OR = 0.42 (95% CI 0.28–0.63; I² = 18%), favoring RAS.

A meta-analysis including the seven studies which reported operative time found significantly longer operations using robotic-assisted surgery (SMD 0.57 [CI 0.31–0.83], p < 0.0001). Nine studies reported conversion-to-open rates, and meta-analysis demonstrated a significantly lower conversion rate in robotic-assisted surgery (OR 0.41 [CI 0.32–0.51], p < 0.00001).

Four studies examined male gender as a high-risk factor and included a total of 934 robotic-assisted cases and 3762 laparoscopic cases [24, 29, 42, 43]. All but one of the studies looked at resections for rectal cancer alone, with the fourth study including all types of colectomies. There were no significant differences between the two groups with regards to complication rate (OR 1.09 [CI 0.91–1.30], p = 0.36) or length of stay (SMD 0.19 [CI − 0.51–0.13], p = 0.25). Operative time was again significantly longer in the robotic-assisted group (SMD 0.77 [CI 0.17–1.37], p = 0.01). However, conversion to open was significantly lower in the robotic-assisted group (OR 0.28 [CI 0.22–0.34], p < 0.00001), Fig. 3.
Of the two studies that reported on conversion to open rates, these were found to be significantly lower in the robotic-assisted group (OR 0.10 [CI 0.02–0.58], p = 0.01).

Conversion to Laparotomy (CtL) was examined by three of the four studies included in our meta-analysis, involving 337 patients: 98 in the RC group and 239 in the LC group [19, 20, 22] Fig. 3. Upon examining the pooled results on conversion to laparotomy, obtained from the meta-analysis, no statistically significant difference emerged between the groups under consideration [Odds Ratio (OR): 0.20, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.04, 1.14, P=0.07].

In the colon subgroup (8 studies), robotic-assisted surgery had significantly lower conversion rates compared to laparoscopy [Risk Ratio (RR): 0.62; 95% CI: 0.52–0.74; p < 0.001; I2 = 50.5%]. The rectum subgroup (12 studies) also had a corresponding benefit for robotic surgery (RR: 0.44; 95% CI: 0.34–0.59; p < 0.001; I2 = 44.3%). In the subgroup for colorectal (4 studies), the trend existed for robotic surgery but the result was not significant (RR: 0.23; 95% CI: 0.05–1.19; p = 0.079; I2 = 61.9%) (Figure 4).

RS had a significantly lower conversion rate in 9 studies included 2614 patients (odds ratio: 0.42; 95% confidence interval: 0.28 to 0.63; P < 0.0001) (Fig. 5), more lymph nodes harvested in 10 studies included 3056 patients (mean difference: 0.67; 95% confidence interval: 0.30 to 1.04; P = 0.0004) (Fig. 6), and a smaller incidence of positive CRM in 6 studies included 2623 patients (odds ratio: 0.59; 95% confidence interval: 0.41 to 0.85; P = 0.004) (Fig. 7).
note: All five meta-analyses were checked. Four report a statistically significant robotic advantage in at least one defined subgroup or overall; Morini reports no significant difference. Gahunia also reports non-significant conversion results in other subgroups.

question: Among the five meta-analyses in this corpus, which included randomised controlled trials only, rather than observational or mixed-design studies?
answer: RCT-only: Muafa (12 RCTs; 3,107 patients) and Zou (11 RCTs; 3,107 cases). Gahunia included randomised and non-randomised studies; Morini included four observational comparative studies; Al-Ihribat included RCTs and cohort studies.
quote: Only RCTs comparing RAS vs. LS for malignant colorectal disease were included. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers. Meta-analyses used DerSimonian–Laird random-effects models; standardized procedures were applied for converting medians/IQRs into means/SDs and for continuity corrections in zero-event trials. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane RoB 2.0, and evidence certainty was graded using GRADE. RESULTS: A total of 12 RCTs encompassing 3,107 patients met the inclusion criteria.
All randomised and non-randomised studies which report original data on any outcome of robotic colorectal surgery in high-risk patients are included.
The 4 included comparative studies (373 patients: 116 robotic colectomy versus 257 laparoscopic colectomy) had a time frame of approximately 26 years (2005–2021) and an observational nature.

From 2018 to December 2024, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were used to perform a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies and randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Studies comparing RAS and conventional laparoscopic surgery were included.
11 RCTs including a total of 3107 cases were identified.

question: Among the five meta-analyses in this corpus, what did each report about length of hospital stay after robotic versus laparoscopic surgery?
answer: Gahunia: obesity subgroup SMD 0.25 (95% CI −0.41 to −0.09), p=0.002, shorter with robotic; male rectal-only sensitivity analysis SMD −0.40 (95% CI −0.75 to 0.06), p=0.02, described as favouring RAS despite the confidence interval crossing zero; Morini: MD −1.11 days (95% CI −2.05, −0.18), p=0.002, shorter with robotic; Al-Ihribat: colon MD −0.59 days, rectum MD −0.68 days, colorectal MD −3.68 days, all significantly shorter with robotic; Muafa: MD −0.8 days (95% CI −1.3 to −0.2), shorter with robotic; Zou: MD −0.68 (95% CI −1.50, 0.14), p=0.10, not significant.
quote: Length of stay showed a small but significant reduction with RAS (MD − 0.8 days; 95% CI − 1.3 to − 0.2; I²=49%).
Six studies reported on length of stay, and meta-analysis suggested a reduced length of stay in patients undergoing robotic-assisted surgery (SMD 0.25 [CI − 0.41 to − 0.09], p = 0.002).

Length of Hospital Stay (LoHS) was examined by all four studies included in our meta-analysis, involving 373 patients: 116 in the RC group and 257 in the LC group [19–22] Fig. 7. Upon examining the pooled results on the LoHS, obtained from the meta-analysis, a statistically significant difference emerged between the groups under consideration [MD: - 1.11, 95%, CI: −2.05, −0.18, P=0.002].

Robot -assisted surgery was found to be linked to shorter hospital stay across all subgroups. In the colon subgroup (8 studies), the reduction was statistically significant (MD: −0.59 days; 95% CI: −0.78 to −0.41; p < 0.001; I2 = 66.4%). The rectum subgroup (10 studies) also demonstrated a shorter stay for robotic procedures (MD: −0.68 days; 95% CI: −1.15 to −0.20; p = 0.005; I2 = 93.2%). In the colorectal subgroup (3 studies), robotic surgery led to significantly greater reduction in hospital stay (MD: −3.68 days; 95% CI: −5.28 to −2.07; p < 0.001; I2 = 92.6%) (Supplementary Figure 6S).

Sensitivity analysis of rectal resections alone did not alter the primary outcome but did alter operative time to be equivalent between the two groups (SMD 0.75 [CI − 0.70 to 2.19] p = 0.31) and length of stay then favoured RAS (SMD − 0.40 [CI − 0.75 to 0.06] p = 0.02).
note: All five meta-analyses are included. Gahunia reports the obesity high-risk subgroup; Al-Ihribat reports anatomical subgroups; Zou reports no statistically significant difference.

question: Among the five meta-analyses in this corpus, what did each report about postoperative complications?
answer: Muafa: CD ≥II complications OR 0.91 (95% CI 0.76–1.13), no significant difference; Gahunia: obesity OR 0.96 (0.81–1.14), p=0.68; male OR 1.09 (0.91–1.30), p=0.36; elderly OR 1.02 (0.59–1.78), p=0.94; low rectal OR 0.94 (0.58–1.52), p=0.81; neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy OR 1.10 (0.66–1.81), p=0.72; previous abdominal surgery OR 0.89 (0.35–2.27), p=0.80; Morini: overall complications MD 0.96 (95% CI 0.57, 1.61), p=0.88, no significant difference; Al-Ihribat: colon RR 0.98 (0.90–1.08), p=0.079, and rectum RR 0.98 (0.83–1.16), p=0.81, not significant; colorectal RR 0.91 (0.84–0.99), p=0.026, fewer with robotic; Zou: overall complications OR 0.86 (0.62, 1.19), p=0.35, no significant difference.

Blood loss (SMD 0.23 [CI − 0.51 to 0.05], p = 0.11), overall complication rate (OR 0.96 [CI 0.81–1.14], p = 0.68), and lymph node yield (SMD 0.11 [CI − 0.07 to 0.28], p = 0.24) were comparable between groups.

Overall Postoperative Complications Rate (OPCR) was examined by all four studies included in our meta-analysis, involving 373 patients: 116 in the RC group and 257 in the LC group [19–22] Fig. 8. Upon examining the pooled results on the OPCR, obtained from the meta-analysis, no statistically significant difference emerged between the groups under consideration [MD: 0.96, 95%, CI: 0.57, 1.61, P=0.88].

In 7 studies of the colon subgroup, the two procedures were not significantly different regarding postoperative complication rates (RR: 0.98; 95% CI: 0.90–1.08; p = 0.079; I2 = 15.6%). in rectum subgroup (11 studies) no significant difference was found (RR: 0.98; 95% CI: 0.83–1.16; p = 0.81; I2 = 54.3%). However, the colorectal subgroup (4 studies) showed significantly fewer complications in the robotic-assisted group (RR: 0.91; 95% CI: 0.84–0.99; p = 0.026; I2 = 0%) (Figure 5).

Pooling the data from 9 studies that assessed overall postoperative complications in 2675 patients showed no significant difference between the RS and LS groups (odds ratio: 0.86; 95% confidence interval: 0.62 to 1.19; P = 0.35) (Fig. 3).

Four studies examined male gender as a high-risk factor and included a total of 934 robotic-assisted cases and 3762 laparoscopic cases [24, 29, 42, 43]. All but one of the studies looked at resections for rectal cancer alone, with the fourth study including all types of colectomies. There were no significant differences between the two groups with regards to complication rate (OR 1.09 [CI 0.91–1.30], p = 0.36) or length of stay (SMD 0.19 [CI − 0.51–0.13], p = 0.25). Operative time was again significantly longer in the robotic-assisted group (SMD 0.77 [CI 0.17–1.37], p = 0.01). However, conversion to open was significantly lower in the robotic-assisted group (OR 0.28 [CI 0.22–0.34], p < 0.00001), Fig. 3.

Operative time was significantly longer in the robotic-assisted group (SMD 0.50 [CI 0.18–0.83], p = 0.002). There was no difference between the two groups with regards to conversion to open (OR 0.28 [CI 0.07–1.11], p = 0.07), complication rate (OR 1.02 [CI 0.59–1.78], p = 0.94), length of stay (SMD 3.20 [CI − 10.45 to 4.06], p = 0.39), estimated blood loss (SMD 0.04 [CI − 0.29 to 0.22], p = 0.77) or lymph node yield (SMD 0.34 [CI − 0.78 to 0.10], p = 0.13).

There was no difference between the two groups with regards to complication rate (OR 0.94 [CI 0.58–1.52], p = 0.81), estimated blood loss (SMD − 0.37 [CI − 0.89 to 0.15], p = 0.16), length of stay (SMD − 0.34 [CI − 0.87 to 0.18], p = 0.20) or lymph node yield SMD − 0.07 [CI − 0.34 to 0.19], p = 0.59).

Seven studies examined patients who had received long-course neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for low rectal cancer, with a total number of 305 robotic-assisted cases and 422 laparoscopic [26, 32, 33, 41, 43, 47, 53], Fig. 3. Operative time was significantly longer in the robotic-assisted group (SMD 0.72 [CI 0.34–1.09], p = 0.0002). There was no difference between the two groups with regards to conversion to open (OR 0.47 [CI 0.09–2.43], p = 0.37), complication rate (OR 1.10 [CI 0.66–1.81], p = 0.72), estimated blood loss (SMD 0.17 [CI − 0.74 to 0.40], p = 0.56), length of stay (SMD 0.07 [CI − 0.22 to 0.08], p = 0.36) or lymph node yield (SMD 0.18 [CI − 0.28 to 0.64], p = 0.44).

Two studies looked at patients who had previous abdominal surgery, with a total number of 274 robotic-assisted cases and 674 laparoscopic [35, 39]. There was no significant difference between the two groups with regards to conversion to open (OR 0.42 [CI 0.08–2.21], p = 0.30), complication rate (OR 0.89 [CI 0.35–2.27], p = 0.80) or length of stay (SMD 0.06 [CI − 0.14 to 0.27], p = 0.54). Again, operative time was significantly longer for RAS (SMD 1.55 [CI 0.05–3.06], p = 0.04), Fig. 3.
